STAT 4102 · Fall 2026 · Wackerly Chapters 7–11

Made Simple

Thirty-seven short lessons that teach the course from the beginning, in plain words. Each one gives you the idea, a recipe, one worked example and a few problems to try.

How each lesson works

  1. ReadStart with The idea. It is short on purpose. Read it slowly, twice if needed.
  2. FollowGo through the worked example with a pencil. Cover the handwritten notes on the right, guess the reason for each step, then uncover.
  3. TryDo Your turn. The first problem has blanks to fill in. The next two you do alone.
  4. CheckCompare with the answers: the Answer Key on paper, or the "Check my answer" button online. If you missed something, reread only that step of the recipe.
  5. KeepCopy the Remember this box by hand. Writing it is what makes it stick.

Short on time?

Exam II is Wednesday, November 18. It covers Parts 3 and 4 (Lessons 9–20). You may bring one page of handwritten notes (both sides) and a scientific calculator. Bring the calculator.

  • Day 1: Lessons 9–14 (efficiency, consistency, Slutsky, method of moments, maximum likelihood, Fisher information).
  • Day 2: Lessons 15–20 (errors, power, Z tests, β and sample size, intervals, p-values).
  • Day 3: Redo every "Your turn" without looking. Write your note page from the "Exam II on one page" sheet at the back. Then work the practice exam.

If a Part 3 or 4 lesson feels confusing, the idea underneath is usually in Lesson 1, 3, 4 or 6. Go back and read that one first.

Parts 5 and 6 (Lessons 21–37) are for Exam III on December 16. Leave them until Exam II is done.

Lesson 1 · Part 1: How samples behaveExam I material

Samples and statistics

Why your average changes every time you take a new sample.

The question

I measured 25 students and got an average. With 25 different students I would get a different average. So how much can I trust mine?

The idea

A population is the whole group you care about. It has true numbers that we cannot see, called parameters, like the true mean ("mu") and the true spread ("sigma").

A sample is the small part we actually measure: . Any number you compute from the sample alone is a statistic. The most famous one is the sample mean ("Y-bar"): add up the data and divide by .

Here is the key idea of the whole course: a statistic is random. A new sample gives a new value. The pattern of values it could take is called its sampling distribution.

For the pattern is simple. It is centered on the true mean, and it is less spread out than single data points:

The recipe

Mean and variance of a combination

  1. Means: add them, and constants come along. .
  2. Variances (independent data): square the constants, then add. .
  3. For an average: the center is and the SD is .

Worked example

Wait times at a bus stop have mean minutes and SD minutes. You record waits. Find the mean, variance and SD of .
  1. The average aims right at the true mean.
  2. Variance uses , so square the 6 first.
  3. minute
    One wait is off by about 6 minutes. An average of 36 waits is off by only about 1.

Averaging 36 waits makes the estimate 6 times steadier, because .

Four famous curves, and when each one shows up.

If my data are bell-shaped, exactly how do the sample mean and the sample variance behave?

The idea

When the data come from a normal (bell-shaped) population, we know the exact sampling distributions. There are four curves to know. Each one answers one kind of question.

The Central Limit Theorem

Averages turn bell-shaped, even when the data are not.

The question

My data are not bell-shaped at all. Can I still use the normal curve?

The idea

Yes, if you are working with an average and the sample is big enough.

Central Limit Theorem (CLT). Take independent data points from any population with mean and SD . When is large, is approximately normal:

Rule of thumb: is large enough.

Two things happen as grows. The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) says closes in on . The CLT says the leftover wobble has a bell shape.

Counts too. A count of yes answers is a sum of 0s and 1s, so the CLT covers proportions: .

The recipe

A CLT probability

  1. Write down and for one data point.
  2. SD of the average .
  3. .
  4. Look up the area in the Z table.

Worked example

Checkout times at a store are skewed, with mean minutes and SD minutes. For customers, find the chance that the average time is above 5.5 minutes.
  1. , so is approximately normal.
    The data are skewed, but an average of 64 is not.
  2. Divide by .
  3. 5.5 is two SDs above the center.
  4. About 2%.

Counts: the 0.5 correction

If Binomial, treat as normal with mean and SD . Counts jump in whole steps, so widen by 0.5: and .

Lesson 4 · Part 2: Estimating an unknown numberExam I material

Bias, variance and MSE

How to grade a guessing rule.

The question

There are many ways to guess an unknown number from data. How do I tell a good way from a bad way?

The idea

An estimator ("theta-hat") is a rule that turns data into a guess for the unknown number . Example: is an estimator of .

Think of a dart player. One throw tells you little. You grade the player over many throws. In the same way, we grade an estimator over many samples.

Bias is about aim. Is the average guess on target? . If the bias is 0, the estimator is unbiased.

Variance is about steadiness. Are the guesses close to each other?

Mean squared error (MSE) gives one overall grade. Smaller is better.

The recipe

Find the bias, variance and MSE

  1. Find with the mean rules.
  2. Bias .
  3. Find with the variance rules.
  4. MSE .

Worked example

A machine draws numbers evenly between 0 and , so Uniform with and . You do not know . Grade the estimator .
  1. The data average sits at , the middle. Doubling it aims at .
  2. Bias
    Unbiased.
  3. Square the 2. And .
  4. MSE
    Unbiased, so the MSE is just the variance.

Unbiased is nice, but it is not everything

The largest data point always sits a little below , so it is biased. But its MSE is , which beats once . A small bias with a much smaller variance can win.

Lesson 5 · Part 2: Estimating an unknown numberExam I material

Standard error

How far off is my estimate, probably?

The question

I have an estimate. It is surely not exactly right. How big is the miss, typically?

The idea

The standard deviation of an estimator has a special name: the standard error (SE). It is the typical size of a miss.

The four estimators below are unbiased and, for large samples, approximately normal (CLT). For a normal curve, about 95% of the area is within 2 SDs of the center. So:

About 95% of the time, the estimate lands within 2 SE of the truth. The number is called the 2-standard-error bound.

To estimateUseStandard error
a mean
a proportion
a difference of means
a difference of proportions

Call this table the Big Four. It comes back in confidence intervals (Lesson 6) and in tests (Lesson 17).

The recipe

Estimate with a 2-SE bound

  1. Pick the row of the Big Four that matches the question.
  2. Compute the estimate.
  3. Compute the SE from the sample numbers.
  4. Report: estimate, give or take .

Worked example

In a random sample of voters, 560 favor Candidate Jones. Estimate the true fraction and give a 2-SE bound.
  1. The sample proportion.
  2. 0.44 is .
  3. Bound
    Two standard errors.

We estimate that 56% favor Jones, and we are about 95% sure the truth is within 3 points of that.

Lesson 6 · Part 2: Estimating an unknown numberExam I material

Confidence intervals

Give a range, and say how sure you are.

The question

Instead of one number, can I give a range that probably contains the truth?

The idea

A confidence interval (CI) is a range built from the data: the estimate minus a margin, up to the estimate plus a margin.

The confidence level (such as 95%) describes the method. If you repeated the study many times, 95% of the intervals you built would contain the true value.

For the Big Four with large samples, the recipe is always the same:

Confidence level90%95%98%99%
1.6451.962.332.58

Why ? The leftover area is split between the two tails.

More confidence gives a wider interval. More data gives a narrower one.

One-sided bound. If you only need a floor (or a ceiling), put all of in one tail and use . Lower bound: estimate .

The recipe

A large-sample confidence interval

  1. Get the estimate and its SE from the Big Four table.
  2. Choose for your confidence level.
  3. Margin .
  4. Interval estimate margin. Say it in words.

Worked example

Shopping times for customers have minutes and . Build a 90% CI for the true mean .
  1. , so
    Take the square root of the variance first.
  2. 90% means
    , half in each tail.
  3. Margin
    z times SE.
  4. Estimate minus and plus the margin.

We are 90% confident the true mean shopping time is between 29.7 and 36.3 minutes.

Lesson 7 · Part 2: Estimating an unknown numberExam I material

Building an interval from scratch

The pivot method: where confidence intervals come from.

The question

The ± formula works for the Big Four. What do I do in other situations?

The idea

Use a pivot. A pivot is a formula that mixes the data with the unknown , and whose distribution is completely known. Its distribution does not depend on .

You already know one: contains the unknown , yet it is always .

Because we know the pivot's distribution, we can trap it between two numbers with any probability we like. Then we do algebra until stands alone in the middle. What is left on the outside is the confidence interval.

Tip. If the parameter shifts the data (like a mean), try a difference such as . If it stretches the data (like in Uniform or an exponential mean), try a ratio such as .

The recipe

The pivot method

  1. Find a pivot : data and mixed together, with a known distribution.
  2. Find and with . Usually put in each tail.
  3. Solve the inequalities for .
  4. The two ends are the interval.

Worked example

You observe one waiting time from an exponential distribution with mean , so . Build a 90% CI for .
  1. Pivot: .
    No is left in the answer, so is a pivot.

  2. 5% in each tail leaves 90% in the middle.
  3. Flip to get on top. Flipping swaps the two ends.
  4. CI:
    If minutes: [2.0, 117]. Very wide, because one data point says little.

More data should bring you closer to the truth.

The question

The idea

An estimator is consistent if, as grows, it gets as close to as you like, with probability going to 1. We write and say "converges in probability to ."

Formal version: for every small tolerance , as .

You almost never prove this from the definition. You use three tools:

  • Law of Large Numbers (LLN). A sample average converges to the population average: . It works for an average of anything, for example .
  • Theorem 9.1. If is unbiased and , then it is consistent. (More generally, MSE is enough.)
  • Theorem 9.2. Limits pass through arithmetic and continuous functions. If and , then , , (when ), and for any continuous .

Match the sample average to the formula, then solve.

The question

The idea

The method of moments (MoM) is the quickest way.

The model gives a formula for the population mean in terms of the unknown parameter. The data give the sample mean . By the LLN they should be about equal. So set them equal and solve for the parameter.

One unknown parameter needs one equation. Two unknowns need two: match the 1st and the 2nd moments.

MoM estimators are usually consistent. The proof is the one from Lesson 10: LLN plus a continuous function.

The question

The idea

Flip a coin 10 times and see 7 heads. Which explains that best? makes 7 heads almost impossible. makes it most likely. So we estimate as 0.7. That is maximum likelihood.

The likelihood is the probability (or density) of your data, viewed as a function of . For independent data it is a product:

The logic of a test

A yes-or-no decision, and the two ways it can go wrong.

The question

Someone makes a claim about a parameter. Do my data give enough evidence against it?

The idea

A hypothesis test works like a court trial. The null hypothesis is the default, like "innocent." The alternative is what you are trying to show, like "guilty." You keep unless the data give strong evidence against it.

Every test has four parts: , , a test statistic (a number computed from the data), and a rejection region (RR): the values of the test statistic that make you reject .

You can be wrong in two ways:

You do not reject You reject

Lesson 19 · Part 4: Testing a claimOn Exam II

Tests and intervals agree

Read a test result straight off a confidence interval.

The question

I already have a confidence interval. Do I need to run a separate test?

The idea

No. A two-sided test at level and a confidence interval always agree:

Reject exactly when is outside the confidence interval.

Why? You fail to reject when . That says the estimate is within SEs of , which is the same as being within SEs of the estimate. And that is the interval.

So a confidence interval is the set of all values that the test would not reject.

The levels must match: a 95% interval goes with , and a 90% interval goes with .

One-sided tests pair with one-sided bounds. For , reject when is below the lower bound . For , reject when is above the upper bound .

The recipe

Test with a confidence interval

  1. Match the levels: two-sided goes with a interval.
  2. Build (or read) the interval.
  3. Is inside? Inside: fail to reject. Outside: reject.

Worked example

  2. Estimate ± z × SE.
  3. Is 0 inside? No.

  4. Reject
    Same answer as the Z test: .

Lesson 20 · Part 4: Testing a claimOn Exam II

p-values

One number that says how strong the evidence is.

The question

Instead of only "reject" or "fail to reject," can I say how strong the evidence is?

The idea

Yes: report the p-value. It is the probability, computed as if is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one you observed.

A small p-value means that what you saw would be rare if were true. That is strong evidence against .

Another way to say it: the p-value is the smallest at which you would reject .

Decision rule: reject when the p-value is .

saysp-value for an observed
, the area to the right
, the area to the left
, both tails

Think of as the amount of evidence you demand, and the p-value as the amount of evidence you got.

The recipe

Find and use a p-value

  1. Compute the test statistic.
  2. Find the tail area in the direction of . Double it for a two-tailed test.
  3. Compare with . If the p-value is , reject .

Two small samples: pool the spread, then use t.

The question

I have two small groups. Is the difference between their averages real, or just luck?

The idea

With small samples you need a statistic, and a statistic needs one estimate of spread.

So assume both populations are normal with the same variance . Then and estimate the same number, and you combine them into the pooled variance:

It is a weighted average: the bigger sample gets more weight.

The test statistic has the usual shape:

The question

The idea

Compare two models.

  • The complete model has all of the terms. Its error sum of squares is .
  • The reduced model keeps only the first of them. Its error sum of squares is .
